etymology: From Latin benedictio — "good word, blessing."
biblical_def: The pronounced blessing closing a worship service; the Aaronic in Numbers 6:24-26 and the apostolic in 2 Corinthians 13:14 are the two great biblical formulas, both Trinitarian in shape.
webster_summary: The pronounced blessing closing worship.
webster_full: The formal pronounced blessing that closes the worship service; the two great biblical formulas are the Aaronic Blessing of Numbers 6 (LORD bless and keep, make face shine and be gracious, lift face and give peace) and the apostolic of 2 Corinthians 13:14 (grace of Christ, love of God, fellowship of Spirit) — both Trinitarian in structure.
scriptures: The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep... Make you perfect in every good work.
corruption_summary: Replaced by 'have a great week' or other casual sendoffs; the formal benediction is a doctrinal-pastoral pronouncement.
corruption_paragraphs: A benediction is not a goodbye — it is a pronouncement of blessing in the name of the triune God. The pastor stands as ambassador. The congregation receives. Recover the formal benediction; it shapes the week and rounds the worship.

etymology: From Latin invocatio — "calling upon."
biblical_def: The opening prayer of worship that calls upon God's name and presence; rooted in the biblical practice of calling upon the LORD (Gen 4:26; Acts 2:21).
webster_summary: The opening prayer calling upon God's presence.
webster_full: The opening prayer of formal worship by which God is invoked — His name called upon, His presence sought, His character honored before the rest of the service unfolds; rooted in the biblical practice of 'calling upon the name of the LORD.'
scriptures: Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.
And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.
corruption_summary: Often skipped or replaced by greetings; Scripture honors the deliberate calling-upon as foundational to worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Worship begins by calling upon God. The invocation is not an opening warm-up; it is the recognition that without His drawing-near, worship cannot occur. Recover the invocation as deliberate, not perfunctory.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara b'shem YHWH — to call upon the name of the LORD.
usage: Worship begins with calling upon God's name.

etymology: Composite term for the opening element of Reformed worship.
biblical_def: The opening element of formal worship in which the congregation is summoned to worship God; typically a Scripture call (Ps 95:6; 100:1-2; 96:7-9) declaring the basis and posture of worship.
webster_summary: Scripture summoning the congregation to worship.
webster_full: The opening element of Reformed worship in which the congregation is summoned to worship God; typically pronounced from a Psalm or other Scripture by the minister, declaring God's worthiness as the basis and the posture (kneel, bow, sing) appropriate to the moment.
scriptures: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker. For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture.
Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness.
corruption_summary: Replaced by announcements or musical 'warm-up'; the call to worship is itself a worship element.
corruption_paragraphs: The call to worship is not preamble; it is participation. God is being honored from the first words. Replace announcements at the front of service with a deliberate Scripture call. The congregation arrives gathered to do business with God.

etymology: Latin votum — "vow, prayer"; Reformed liturgical term for the opening declaration of dependence.
biblical_def: The opening declaration of dependence in classical Reformed worship: 'Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth' (Ps 124:8) — a brief vow placing the worship under God's name.
webster_summary: The Reformed opening declaration of dependence.
webster_full: The opening element in classical Reformed worship — a brief vow drawn from Psalm 124:8 ('Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth') placing the gathered service under God's covenant name; precedes the salutation of grace.
scriptures: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Lost in many evangelical services; the votum's confession of dependence orients the whole service rightly.
corruption_paragraphs: The votum is one verse spoken at the start: our help is in the name of the LORD. Spoken weekly, it shapes a congregation's entire spiritual posture. Recover this small Reformed treasure.
usage: Our help is in the name of the LORD.

etymology: From Latin salutatio — "greeting."
biblical_def: The pastor's pronouncement of grace and peace at the start of worship in the name of the triune God; modeled by Paul's epistolary openings ('grace and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ').
webster_summary: Pastor's pronouncement of grace and peace.
webster_full: The pastor's pronouncement of grace and peace from the triune God at the opening of worship; modeled by Paul's epistolary openings ('grace and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ'); functions in worship as the apostolic word descending to the congregation.
scriptures: Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be unto you, and peace, from him which is, and which was, and which is to come; and from the seven Spirits which are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Replaced by casual 'good morning, everyone' rather than the apostolic pronouncement of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not open his letters with 'how are you' — he opens with grace and peace pronounced. The salutation in worship carries the same weight: the congregation is greeted in the name of the triune God. Recover the apostolic salutation.
roots_summary: Greek charis kai eirēnē — grace and peace.

etymology: From Latin confessio — "acknowledgment."
biblical_def: Public declaration of what one believes; biblically the open confession 'Jesus is Lord' (Rom 10:9-10) and historically the great Reformed confessions (Westminster, Belgic, Heidelberg, Second London).
webster_summary: Public declaration of biblical doctrine.
webster_full: The public declaration of what one believes; biblically the open confession 'Jesus is Lord, raised from the dead'; historically the great Reformed and Lutheran confessional documents (Westminster, Belgic, Heidelberg, Augsburg, Second London) that summarized biblical doctrine for the church's instruction and unity.
scriptures: If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
Lay hold on eternal life... and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering.
corruption_summary: Replaced by 'no creed but Christ' which itself is a creed; the confessions guard the faith across generations.
corruption_paragraphs: A church without a confession has a confession; it is just hidden, vague, and unaccountable. Written confessions guard the faith and serve teaching. The Reformed confessions are catechetical treasure. Use them.
usage: Use written confessions; do not invent in private.

etymology: Modern liturgical term for alternating Scripture reading.
biblical_def: The congregational practice of alternating Scripture reading between leader and people; rooted in the Psalms' antiphonal structure (Pss 24, 118, 136) and the temple choirs.
webster_summary: Alternating Scripture reading between leader and people.
webster_full: The congregational practice of alternating Scripture reading between leader and people, or between two parts of the assembly; rooted in the antiphonal structure of many Psalms (especially 24, 118, 136 with its 'for his mercy endureth for ever' refrain) and in the temple choirs.
scriptures: O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Lift up your heads, O ye gates... Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty.
And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God. And all the people answered, Amen, Amen, with lifting up their hands: and they bowed their heads, and worshipped the LORD.
corruption_summary: Lost in churches that fear formal liturgy as 'cold,' missing the ancient warmth of corporate Scripture-engagement.
corruption_paragraphs: Responsive reading is ancient. The Psalms were written for it. Nehemiah 8 shows the assembly answering Ezra. Recover the practice — it builds Scripture into the congregation's bones.

etymology: From Latin collecta — "gathered prayer," the prayer that gathers the people's intentions.
biblical_def: A short, structured prayer with five parts (address, attribute, petition, purpose, mediation) used in liturgical worship to focus congregational prayer; widely used since the early church.
webster_summary: Short structured prayer of liturgical worship.
webster_full: A short, structured prayer used in liturgical worship to focus congregational prayer; classical structure: address to God, attribute of God recalled, petition asked, purpose stated, and pleading 'through Jesus Christ our Lord.' Many fine examples in the Book of Common Prayer.
scriptures: And when they heard that, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, Lord, thou art God... grant unto thy servants, that with all boldness they may speak thy word.
Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Dismissed as Anglican rote; missing how the structure trains good prayer-shape.
corruption_paragraphs: The collect form is excellent training: address God specifically, recall what He is, ask for what fits, name the purpose, plead through Christ. Even free-prayer churches benefit from learning the structure. Pray collectedly.
usage: Pray collectedly: address, attribute, petition, purpose, mediation.

etymology: Composite term for the corporate confession of sin in worship.
biblical_def: The corporate confession of sin in worship — congregation acknowledging their sins to God in unity; rooted in Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9, Ezra 9, and Psalm 51.
webster_summary: Congregation's united confession of sin in worship.
webster_full: The corporate confession of sin in worship by which the congregation acknowledges its sins to God in unity; rooted in the great corporate confessions of Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9, Ezra 9, and Psalm 51; followed in classical Reformed liturgy by the assurance of pardon.
scriptures: We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments.
Howbeit thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly.
Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness... Against thee, thee only, have I sinned.
corruption_summary: Often replaced with 'silent confession' or skipped; the corporate spoken confession was the historic Christian and Old Testament practice.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 9, Nehemiah 9, Ezra 9 — corporate confession in voiced detail. The assembly speaks together. The pattern shapes the soul. Recover spoken corporate confession; it is one of the most powerful elements of historic worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew yadah — to confess; Greek exomologeō — to confess fully.

etymology: Reformed liturgical element following the prayer of confession.
biblical_def: The Scripture-based pronouncement of God's forgiveness following the prayer of confession; declaring on the basis of Christ's atoning work that those who have confessed are pardoned (1 John 1:9; Ps 103:12; Mic 7:19).
webster_summary: Scripture pronouncement of forgiveness after confession.
webster_full: The Scripture-based pronouncement of God's forgiveness immediately following the prayer of confession in classical Reformed worship; declaring on the basis of Christ's finished work that those who have confessed are forgiven, cleansed, and accepted; typically drawn from 1 John 1:9, Psalm 103, Micah 7, or similar.
scriptures: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
corruption_summary: Skipped entirely so confession leaves the congregation under guilt; the assurance is the gospel-half of the pair.
corruption_paragraphs: Confession without assurance is half the gospel. Romans tells us we are forgiven; the assurance pronounces it weekly. Without it, the congregation can leave still in the dust. With it, they leave standing in grace. Pair them always.

etymology: Composite from liturgy + calendar; the Christian year shaped around the gospel events.
biblical_def: The Christian year structured around the events of redemption — Advent, Christmas, Epiphany, Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, Trinity, Ordinary Time — guiding congregational reading and reflection.
webster_summary: The Christian year structured around redemption events.
webster_full: The structured Christian year shaped around the events of redemption — Advent (anticipation), Christmas (incarnation), Epiphany (revelation), Lent (preparation), Holy Week (Passion), Easter (resurrection), Ascension, Pentecost (Spirit), Trinity (doctrine), Ordinary Time (discipleship); ancient practice rooted in the Jewish calendar's structure of remembrance.
scriptures: Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years. I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain.
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
corruption_summary: Either rejected wholesale (in low-church traditions) or treated superstitiously (in some sacramentalist practice); Romans 14 finds a middle path.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 14 says we may esteem days alike or differently as conscience permits. Where the calendar feeds gospel-formed meditation through the year, it is a gift. Where it becomes mandate or magic, it is the danger Galatians warns of. Use it as servant, not master.
usage: Use the liturgical calendar as servant.

etymology: From Latin adventus — "coming, arrival."
biblical_def: The four-week season of preparation before Christmas, focusing on Christ's first coming in humility and second coming in glory; readings center on prophets, John the Baptist, and Mary.
webster_summary: The four-week preparation for Christmas.
webster_full: The four-Sunday season of preparation for Christmas, focused on Christ's two comings — His first in humility at Bethlehem and His second in glory at the consummation; traditional readings include Old Testament prophecies, John the Baptist's ministry, and Mary's Magnificat.
scriptures: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given.
Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.
Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
corruption_summary: Reduced to commercial Christmas-prep season, missing Advent's distinct second-coming emphasis.
corruption_paragraphs: Advent is not just pre-Christmas. It is two-coming season: the first coming celebrated and the second coming awaited. The classic Advent hymn 'O come, O come, Emmanuel' looks both ways. Recover the eschatological half of Advent.
usage: Advent looks two ways: first and second coming.

etymology: From Greek epiphaneia — "manifestation, appearing."
biblical_def: The Christian season after Christmas (January 6 onward) celebrating the manifestation of Christ to the nations — through the magi, His baptism, and the wedding at Cana.
webster_summary: Season celebrating Christ's manifestation to the nations.
webster_full: The Christian season beginning January 6 celebrating the manifestation (epiphaneia) of Christ to the world — chiefly the visit of the magi (Christ revealed to the Gentiles), His baptism (declared the beloved Son), and the wedding at Cana (His glory manifested in the first sign).
scriptures: And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him.
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory.
corruption_summary: Forgotten in evangelical churches; the rich Christological themes of the season are missed.
corruption_paragraphs: Epiphany season says: Christ has come — and now He is shown. Magi see; Father declares; first sign reveals. The season trains the church to expect ongoing manifestation of Christ in our seeing of Him through Scripture and Spirit.
usage: Epiphany trains expectation of seeing Christ.

etymology: From Old English lencten — "spring," the lengthening of days.
biblical_def: The forty-day Christian season of preparation before Easter, marked by fasting, repentance, prayer, and almsgiving; modeled on Christ's forty days in the wilderness.
webster_summary: Forty-day preparation for Easter.
webster_full: The forty-day Christian season (excluding Sundays) before Easter, marked by fasting, repentance, prayer, and almsgiving; modeled on Christ's forty days of wilderness fasting and the Old Testament forty-day pattern of Moses and Elijah; begins with Ash Wednesday and climaxes in Holy Week.
scriptures: And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred.
Therefore also now, saith the LORD, turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.
Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free.
corruption_summary: Reduced to 'giving up chocolate'; biblical fasting is broader and richer.
corruption_paragraphs: Lent is not minor self-denial; it is forty days of intensified gospel preparation. The pattern: turn to God with fasting, with weeping, with mourning. Use it as servant, not legalism. The point is the Easter destination.
usage: Use Lent for intensified gospel preparation.
Forty days; not legalism; servant of Easter.

etymology: Greek Pentekostē — fiftieth.
biblical_def: The fiftieth day after Easter Sunday, commemorating the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the church (Acts 2); often the beginning of an extended season called Pentecost or Trinity.
webster_summary: Fiftieth day after Easter; Spirit-outpouring.
webster_full: The fiftieth day after Easter Sunday, commemorating the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the gathered disciples in Acts 2; in the liturgical calendar often the start of an extended season (Trinity / Pentecost) running to Advent.
scriptures: And when the day of Pentecost was fully come... they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.
But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost... shall teach you all things.
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.
corruption_summary: Marginalized in much of Western Christianity; the Spirit-poured-out day deserves the same weight as Christmas and Easter.
corruption_paragraphs: Pentecost is the third great Christian feast — incarnation, resurrection, and Spirit-outpouring. Most evangelical churches celebrate the first two and skip the third. Recover Pentecost as a major day; the Spirit's coming is gospel-history, not liturgical decoration.
usage: Celebrate Pentecost as a major feast.
Three coordinate feasts: Christmas, Easter, Pentecost.

etymology: Liturgical season beginning Trinity Sunday (the Sunday after Pentecost).
biblical_def: The long season of the church year beginning Trinity Sunday (the Sunday after Pentecost) running through Advent — focused on the Christian's growth in discipleship under triune grace; also called Ordinary Time.
webster_summary: Long season of discipleship under triune grace.
webster_full: The long season of the church year beginning Trinity Sunday — the Sunday after Pentecost — running through Christ the King Sunday and into Advent; focused on growth in discipleship under triune grace; alternative name for Ordinary Time in some traditions.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.
Till we all come in the unity of the faith... unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
corruption_summary: Often the most-skipped season; pastors lean on holiday seasons but the long discipleship season is where formation happens.
corruption_paragraphs: Christmas and Easter are the bookends; Trinity Season is the long road of formation between. Most growth happens here. Pastors who teach hardest in this 'ordinary' time disciple deepest.
usage: Teach hard during the long Trinity season.

etymology: Latin tempus per annum — "time through the year."
biblical_def: The non-festal weeks of the Christian year — between Epiphany and Lent, and between Pentecost/Trinity and Advent — when readings cycle through ordinary teaching of the gospels and epistles.
webster_summary: Non-festal Sundays of routine discipleship.
webster_full: The non-festal weeks of the Christian year — between Epiphany and Lent, and between Pentecost/Trinity and Advent — when readings cycle through teaching portions of the gospels, epistles, and Old Testament; the discipleship-rhythm of the calendar.
scriptures: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season.
corruption_summary: Treated as boring filler between holiday seasons; the formation-work happens here.
corruption_paragraphs: The word ordinary here means 'numbered / counted' (ordinal time) — not boring. These are the weeks where the church teaches steadily through the gospels and epistles. Faithful preaching in ordinary time builds the church Christmas and Easter sermons can never reach alone.

etymology: From Latin mandatum — "commandment," referencing John 13:34's 'new commandment' given the night of the Last Supper.
biblical_def: The Thursday of Holy Week commemorating the Last Supper, foot-washing, and Christ's new commandment to love one another (John 13).
webster_summary: Thursday of Holy Week; Last Supper and new commandment.
webster_full: The Thursday of Holy Week commemorating Christ's last supper with His disciples, His washing of their feet, and His giving of the new commandment ('A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another' — John 13:34) from which the day takes its name (mandatum).
scriptures: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples.
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
corruption_summary: Forgotten in many evangelical churches; the foot-washing and new commandment of Holy Week deserve their own meditation.
corruption_paragraphs: The night before the cross, Jesus washed feet, instituted the Supper, and gave the new commandment. Maundy Thursday holds these together. To skip from Palm Sunday to Easter loses the upper-room theology that grounds Christian community.
usage: Observe Maundy Thursday for the upper-room theology.

etymology: Christian designation for the day between Good Friday and Easter Sunday.
biblical_def: The Sabbath between Christ's crucifixion and resurrection; the day He rested in the tomb after declaring 'It is finished'; included in the creedal 'descended into hell' or 'descended to the dead.'
webster_summary: The day Christ rested in the tomb.
webster_full: The Sabbath between Christ's crucifixion and resurrection; the day He rested in the tomb after declaring 'It is finished'; included in the Apostles' Creed as 'He descended into hell' or 'descended to the dead' — variously interpreted across traditions but agreeing that Christ truly died and entered the realm of the dead.
scriptures: And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock.
And that day was the preparation, and the sabbath drew on... And they returned, and prepared spices and ointments; and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment.
Christ also hath once suffered for sins... Being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison.
corruption_summary: Treated as empty waiting; Holy Saturday is the day Christ rested His finished work, the great sabbath.
corruption_paragraphs: Holy Saturday is the great sabbath. Christ rested His finished work as the Father rested creation week. The disciples could not see the joy yet. Sometimes faith is sitting at the tomb on the seventh day, trusting the eighth will come.
usage: Holy Saturday is the great sabbath.
Faith sits at the tomb trusting the eighth day.

etymology: Forty days after Easter, commemorating Christ's bodily ascension to the Father (Acts 1:9-11).
biblical_def: The Christian observance forty days after Easter commemorating Christ's bodily ascension from the Mount of Olives to the Father's right hand; the enthronement of the Mediator King.
webster_summary: Forty days after Easter; Christ's bodily ascension.
webster_full: The Christian observance forty days after Easter commemorating Christ's bodily ascension from the Mount of Olives to the Father's right hand, fulfilling the prediction 'I go to my Father'; observed as a major day in Eastern and Western liturgical traditions but largely forgotten in evangelicalism.
scriptures: When he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight... this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner.
And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven.
When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.
corruption_summary: Forgotten in much of evangelicalism; Ascension Day deserves equal weight with Easter and Pentecost.
corruption_paragraphs: Without Ascension, Easter's Christ is wandering. Ascension is the enthronement; the throne; the Father's seat at His right hand; the intercession that secures our prayers. Recover Ascension Day; tell the church the King is enthroned.
usage: Christ enthroned at the Father's right hand.

etymology: The last Sunday of the Christian year (before Advent), focused on Christ's universal kingship.
biblical_def: The final Sunday of the liturgical year (instituted in 1925 to confess Christ's kingship over all earthly powers) celebrating Christ as King of kings and Lord of lords; rounds the Christian year before Advent begins anew.
webster_summary: Last Sunday of the year; Christ's universal kingship.
webster_full: The final Sunday of the Christian year (instituted by Pius XI in 1925 in response to rising secular nationalisms) confessing Christ's kingship over all earthly powers, all nations, and all human history; rounds the Christian year before Advent begins again.
scriptures: And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him... that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.
And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth.
corruption_summary: Forgotten in most evangelical settings; the confession of Christ's kingship over politics and culture is gospel-essential.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ the King Sunday was instituted to confess Christ above Mussolini, Hitler, and the rising tyrannies. The confession is perpetual: every age has its idols. Ending the year with Christ enthroned over all powers is gospel-formation work.
roots_summary: Greek basileus tōn basileōn — King of kings.
usage: Confess Christ's kingship over earthly powers.
End the year with the King enthroned.

etymology: Protestant observance of the Sunday on or before October 31, commemorating Luther's 1517 posting of the 95 Theses.
biblical_def: The Protestant observance commemorating Luther's October 31, 1517 posting of the 95 Theses on the Wittenberg church door; celebrating the recovery of the gospel, the five solas, and Scripture's authority.
webster_summary: Sunday commemorating Luther's 95 Theses.
webster_full: The Protestant observance commemorating the Reformation — typically the Sunday on or before October 31, the date of Luther's 1517 posting of the 95 Theses; a day for celebrating the gospel's recovery, the five solas, and Scripture's authority restored.
scriptures: For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation... For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God.
corruption_summary: Reduced to triumphalism; the right note is gratitude for the gospel, not animus against Catholics.
corruption_paragraphs: Reformation Sunday is for gratitude, not pride. The gospel was recovered; we are recipients, not heroes. Mark the day; teach the solas; pray for ongoing reformation. Always reforming.
usage: Teach the five solas on Reformation Sunday.

etymology: From Latin festum omnium sanctorum — "feast of all saints."
biblical_def: The November 1 observance honoring the cloud of witnesses — the faithful departed believers who have run the race ahead of us — drawn from Hebrews 11-12 and Revelation 7.
webster_summary: November 1; remembering the faithful departed.
webster_full: The November 1 observance honoring the cloud of witnesses — all faithful believers who have died in Christ and now stand before the throne; rooted in Hebrews 11's roll of faith and Hebrews 12's 'cloud of witnesses' and Revelation 7's great multitude.
scriptures: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.
After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne.
And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise: God having provided some better thing for us, that they without us should not be made perfect.
corruption_summary: Sometimes confused with prayers for the dead (which the Reformers rejected); the right use is gratitude and emulation.
corruption_paragraphs: Reformed All Saints does not pray for the dead; it gives thanks for them and seeks to imitate their faith. Hebrews 12 tells us we are surrounded; the day reminds us we are not running alone. Mark the day; honor faithful saints; press on.
usage: Give thanks for the saints who have run.
Imitate their faith; do not pray to them.

etymology: Opening words of the great early Christian hymn — Te Deum laudamus — "We praise Thee, O God."
biblical_def: The early Christian hymn (4th-5th century) traditionally attributed to Ambrose and Augustine; a Trinitarian doxology used at major Christian celebrations and victories.
webster_summary: Ancient Christian hymn 'We praise Thee, O God.'
webster_full: The great early Christian hymn opening with Te Deum laudamus ('We praise Thee, O God'); traditionally ascribed to Ambrose and Augustine in the 4th-5th century; a Trinitarian doxology celebrating God's glory, used historically at major Christian celebrations, military victories, and times of national thanksgiving.
scriptures: And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come.
Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
corruption_summary: Faded from common congregational use; the great hymn deserves recovery.
corruption_paragraphs: The Te Deum is one of the great hymns of the Christian centuries — sung at Pentecost, at Christmas, at thanksgivings, at victories. Read its text; it is a doctrinally rich doxology unmatched in modern worship songs. Worth reintroducing.
usage: It is a doctrinal doxology rare in modern worship.

etymology: Greek Kyrie eleison (Κύριε ἐλέησον) — "Lord, have mercy."
biblical_def: The plea 'Lord, have mercy' that runs through the Psalms (Ps 4:1; 6:2; 41:4) and the gospels (the blind men, the Canaanite woman, the publican); incorporated into Christian liturgy as the Kyrie.
webster_summary: "Lord, have mercy" — the great biblical plea.
webster_full: The Greek phrase 'Lord, have mercy' that runs throughout Scripture as the great plea of the needy — David in the Psalms, the blind men of Jericho, the Canaanite woman, the publican in the temple; preserved in Christian liturgy from the earliest centuries as the Kyrie, often sung threefold (Lord have mercy, Christ have mercy, Lord have mercy).
scriptures: And he cried, saying, Jesus, thou Son of David, have mercy on me.
Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.
And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner.
corruption_summary: Rejected by some as 'Catholic,' missing how thoroughly biblical the cry is.
corruption_paragraphs: Kyrie eleison is in the gospel mouth of every needy soul who came to Christ. To dismiss it as ritual is to dismiss the cry of the publican. Pray it; sing it; let it shape the soul. Lord, have mercy.
